activities.name: philReclaimJudge

statements.s: In philosophy, an argument is a quarrel.
statements.why: It is a structure: claims offered as support for another claim.

statements.s: Learn to identify, test and dismantle arguments and you have learned the skill every field borrows from philosophy.
statements.why: The language of argumentation is the discipline's core toolkit — the most directly transferable content in the subject.

statements.s: Philosophy asks the questions every other field must assume answers to.
statements.why: What counts as an explanation, fairness, knowledge — the physicist, the judge and you all assume answers to these.

activities.anchor: the commonest reading failure is treating assertion as argument
activities.caption: sort the signposts
activities.name: philMarkersSort

buckets: not arguing — report, command or description

items.label: "therefore, so, thus, hence, it follows that"
"you should get vaccinated" — the claim the passage wants accepted
"because, since, given that, for the reason that"
"the vaccine trial showed 95% efficacy" — the reason offered
reports, descriptions and commands — they state or order, but do not infer

config.why: Spotting that a reason was given, and what it was, is half of critical thinking.

activities.anchor: which is why philosophical training is double
activities.caption: find the faulty line — argument structure
activities.name: philReconSpot

config.prompt: One line of this gloss on argument structure is wrong — click it:
lines: Standardised: premise 1, premise 2, therefore conclusion — the inference is the only strictly logical part.
Check the inference (logic) and check the premises — philosophical training is double.
Hidden premises should stay hidden: writing them in adds clutter and distorts the argument.
"She was in Paris at noon and in Rome at two — so she flew" quietly assumes travel time.
Making hidden premises explicit is where most analysis happens.
config.correction: Hidden premises should be written in explicitly — they are where unsound arguments hide their work, which is why reconstruction is the first move of serious criticism.
config.why: The soundness fight usually lives in the smuggled premise, not the flashy ones.

config.prompt: Rebuild the classroom-phones reconstruction, then audit it:
items: Premise 1: phones present in classrooms undermine focus
Premise 2: focus is essential for learning
Hidden premise: anything that undermines what is essential for learning should be banned
Conclusion: phones should be banned in classrooms
The audit: the inference is valid — the soundness fight lives in the hidden premise
config.why: Does anything that undermines focus warrant a ban — uncomfortable chairs? a dull lecture? The smuggled premise is where the argument actually lives.

activities.anchor: Each form has its own failure modes
activities.caption: pair each form with its claim
activities.name: philFormsMatch

config.prompt: Three canonical shapes — pair each form with its claim:

pairs.right: claims necessity — the conclusion cannot exceed the premises
claims probability from observed cases to unobserved ones — never guaranteed
reasons from an observation to the hypothesis that would best account for it

pairs.left: demanding deductive certainty from an induction
pairs.right: a category error — each form has its own failure modes

config.why: Diagnosis, detective work and theory choice live in abduction — and offering an induction where a deduction was promised is a cheat.

activities.anchor: confusing them is the classic beginner error
activities.caption: drag the divider — the two verdicts
activities.name: philValidCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — the two verdicts:

before.label: Valid and unsound
before.text: "All fish can fly; Nemo is a fish; therefore Nemo can fly" — the logic is flawless; the premises are fiction.

after.label: Invalid though every statement true
after.text: "All cats are animals; some animals are black; therefore some cats are black" — the form licenses the move no more than a broken bridge licenses crossing.

config.why: When a real argument fails you want to know where — bad logic (fix the form) or bad premises (fix the facts).

config.q: The conclusion turns out true. Was the argument any good?
choices: Yes — it landed on the truth, which is what arguments are for
No — the argument is the route, not the destination; a true conclusion can rest on invalid logic or false premises
config.why: The broken clock reads right twice a day — grade the route.

activities.caption: walk the conditional moves and the razor
activities.name: philRazorSteps

steps.math: If P then Q; P; therefore Q

steps.note: Modus tollens — valid, the form behind every experimental falsification.

steps.math: If P then Q; Q; therefore P
steps.note: Affirming the consequent — invalid; the formal name for the detective's classic error.
Between two explanations accounting equally well for the data, prefer the one with fewer assumptions — a methodological preference, not a truth-guarantee; sometimes the extra entity is real.
